the-starry-night

Van Gogh painted this from memory while staying in a hospital in southern France, and the swirling sky seems to be alive with energy. Instead of copying what he saw, he painted how the night felt: glowing stars, a rolling wind and a sleepy village below. The bold, curling brushstrokes were revolutionary, and they showed artists they could paint emotions, not just objects. Today it is one of the most recognized paintings on Earth.
liberty-leading-the-people

A woman holding the French flag charges over a barricade, with people of every background following her. Delacroix painted it after the 1830 July Revolution in Paris, and it turned a real uprising into a symbol of freedom. The drama, color and movement made it a landmark of Romantic painting. Its image of Liberty has inspired posters, stamps, and even the Statue of Liberty's story.
the-potato-eaters

Van Gogh wanted to show how poor farmers really lived, so he painted a family sharing a humble meal of potatoes by lamplight. The dark, earthy colors and rough faces were deliberate: he wanted to honor honest work with hands that dug the food they ate. It was his first big masterpiece, painted long before his famous bright colors. It reminds us that great art can be about ordinary, hardworking people.
impression-sunrise

Monet painted the misty port of Le Havre at dawn, with a small orange sun and boats made of just a few quick strokes. When critics saw it in 1874, one mockingly said it was only an 'impression' — and the name Impressionism was born! The painting captures a fleeting moment of light instead of fine details. It launched a whole movement that changed how people think about painting.
the-kiss

Two lovers are wrapped together in a golden robe, covered in glittering patterns, kneeling on a flower-dotted meadow. Klimt used real gold leaf, which makes the painting shimmer like a jewel. He mixed flat, decorative patterns with soft, realistic faces and hands. It became the most famous work of the Vienna Secession and is loved around the world as a picture of tenderness.
the-death-of-socrates

The ancient Greek thinker Socrates was sentenced to drink poison, and David shows him calmly raising a finger to make one last point while friends weep around him. The clear, sculpture-like figures and calm lighting made it a model of Neoclassical painting. It is famous because it makes a big idea — standing up for your beliefs, even at great cost — feel real and powerful.
wanderer-above-the-sea-of-fog

A lone traveler stands on a rocky peak with his back to us, gazing over a sea of mist and mountains. Friedrich wanted us to stand in his place and feel awe at nature's size and mystery. It has become the icon of Romanticism, the idea that nature and personal feelings matter deeply. We still know it because everyone has felt like that tiny wanderer at some big, quiet view.
the-raft-of-the-medusa

In 1816 a French ship wrecked, and a handful of survivors drifted on a raft for almost two weeks. Géricault painted the moment they spot rescue far away, using huge, life-size figures and dramatic light. He even studied real survivors to get the details right. The painting was a sensation, turning a news story into a timeless picture of hope and survival against terrible odds.
reply-of-the-zaporozhian-cossacks

According to legend, a band of Cossack warriors received an insulting demand from the Turkish sultan to surrender, and they responded with a joke-filled, rude letter. Repin shows them roaring with laughter as the scribe writes. It took him over a decade, and the laughing faces are so lively you can almost hear them. It's beloved in Ukraine and Russia for its humor and spirit.
la-maja-desnuda

Goya painted a woman reclining on a couch, looking directly at the viewer in a way that was bold and unusual for its time. The painting got him into trouble with the Spanish Inquisition, which only added to its fame. It is remembered for its honest, real-person feeling instead of the idealized goddesses artists usually painted. It's also famously paired with a clothed twin, La maja vestida.
luncheon-on-the-grass

Manet showed a picnic in the woods where two men in everyday suits sit with a woman who isn't dressed for the occasion — and the Paris art world was shocked. Everyone expected nudes to be goddesses from myths, not modern people at lunch. It was rejected from the official show in 1863, then displayed in the famous 'Salon of the Rejected.' It marks a turning point toward modern art.
the-third-of-may-1808

A firing squad aims at a man in a white shirt who raises his arms, while others wait their turn in the dark. Goya painted this to remember Spanish citizens who were executed after standing up to Napoleon's army. He used a glowing lantern and a faceless line of soldiers to make the cruelty of war feel real. It's considered one of the first truly modern anti-war paintings.
bal-du-moulin-de-la-galette

On a sunny Sunday in Montmartre, Parisians dance and chat under trees dappled with light. Renoir painted it on the spot with his friends as models, capturing the happiness of an ordinary afternoon. The flickering spots of sunlight on clothing are a hallmark of Impressionism. It's famous for making you feel as if you've joined the party, and it's one of the most valuable paintings ever sold.
wheatfield-with-crows

A golden field under a stormy blue sky, with a path that seems to run out and crows swirling overhead. Van Gogh painted it in the final weeks of his life, and many people read deep feelings of loneliness in it. Whatever he meant, the wild brushwork and bold color are unforgettable. It's often shown as the ultimate example of how painting can carry strong emotion.
olympia

A woman reclines on a bed, looking straight at us, with a maid bringing flowers and a black cat at her feet. Manet's frank, flat style and her confident gaze scandalized visitors in 1865; some even tried to attack it. Instead of a polite myth, he painted a real modern woman who isn't shy. Today it is seen as a brave starting point of modern art.
irises

Van Gogh painted these irises in the garden of the hospital where he was staying. The purple blooms rise and bend across a sea of green, with one lonely white flower standing out. The bold outlines were inspired by Japanese woodblock prints, which he adored. It sold for a record-setting price in 1987 and remains one of the most beloved flower paintings ever.
the-oath-of-the-horatii

Three brothers in ancient Rome stretch out their arms to swear to fight for their city, while the women of the family weep. David's sharp lines, stage-like setting and strong sense of duty were a stunning change from the frilly paintings that came before. It helped create Neoclassicism and was admired in the years before the French Revolution as a picture of courage and sacrifice.
the-death-of-marat

Jean-Paul Marat, a French revolutionary, lies in his bathtub after being stabbed, clutching a letter in his hand. David was his friend, and he painted it like a sacred picture, with quiet light and an empty background. It's famous because it turned a news event into a haunting memorial. The painting shows how art can shape how people remember history.
cafe-terrace-at-night

A warm yellow glow from a café spills onto cobblestones beneath a deep blue night sky full of stars. Van Gogh painted this in Arles, France, and it was among the first times he painted night without using black. The contrast of orange light against blue is a joy to the eye. It still makes people want to sit down and enjoy an evening there.
a-bar-at-the-folies-bergere

A barmaid stands in front of a mirror at a busy Paris nightclub, looking sad and distant while the crowd sparkles behind her. Manet painted it near the end of his life, and the mirror reflection doesn't quite match what we'd expect, which still puzzles people. It captures the buzz of modern city life and the loneliness inside it. It's one of the great mysteries of art.
the-blue-boy

A young man in a shimmering blue satin suit stands proudly against a stormy landscape. Gainsborough painted it partly to prove he could use blue as a main color — something many artists of his day believed was a mistake. It became hugely famous, and in 1922 it was shipped from England to California, drawing crowds who came to say goodbye. It's a classic of British portrait painting.
the-night-cafe

Van Gogh painted a late-night café in Arles with clashing reds and greens and harsh lamps glowing. He said he wanted to show a place where people could 'ruin themselves, go mad or commit a crime.' The bold colors are meant to feel uneasy. It's famous as an example of how colors alone can create a mood, and it changed the way many artists used them.
the-coronation-of-napoleon

Napoleon, in 1804, took the crown from the Pope and placed it on his own head — and then crowned his wife Josephine, which is the moment David painted. It is enormous, about 10 meters wide, and packed with 200 life-size people. David was Napoleon's official painter, and the picture was meant to show power and glory. It's still a famous record of one of history's biggest ceremonies.
starry-night-over-the-rhone

Gas lamps shimmer in long golden reflections on the river as the Big Dipper glitters overhead and a couple strolls on the shore. Van Gogh painted it outdoors at night in Arles, perhaps with candles on his hat for light. It's calmer and more peaceful than his later Starry Night, and many people consider it just as beautiful. It shows his love of the night sky.
the-ninth-wave

Survivors of a shipwreck cling to a broken mast as a giant wave, the 'ninth wave' of sailors' legend, rises before them — but sunrise lights the sky with hope. Aivazovsky painted the sea so glowing and real that people felt the spray. He is Russia's most beloved painter of the ocean, and this canvas is his best-known work. It's famous for its drama and its message that hope returns with the dawn.
saturn-devouring-his-son

Goya painted this dark picture of the Roman god Saturn on the wall of his own house, never meant for anyone else to see. It's based on a myth in which a king fears his children will replace him. The wild eyes and gloomy darkness make it one of the most intense images in art. It's famous because it shows how artists can explore fear and madness — be warned, it's scary!
the-church-at-auvers

A twisting, wavy church stands against a deep blue sky while a woman walks on a path beside it. Van Gogh painted it in 1890, just weeks before his death, and the building almost seems alive. The strong cobalt blue sky and the curving lines give ordinary architecture a dreamlike feel. It's loved because it turns a small village church into something powerful and unforgettable.
black-square-1915

It is exactly what it sounds like: a black square on a white background. Malevich showed it in 1915 and called it a new beginning for painting, free of any picture of the real world. He wanted art to be about pure feeling and shape. People still argue about it, and that's why it is famous: it asked 'what is art?' and changed painting forever.
the-red-vineyard

Workers in a vineyard carry baskets of grapes under a blazing orange sun, with the whole field glowing red and gold. Van Gogh painted it in Arles in 1888. For a long time it was believed to be the only painting he sold during his life, though that is now thought to be uncertain. It remains famous for its heat and bright, joyful colors.
the-yellow-house

This is the actual house in Arles, France, where Van Gogh lived and hoped to start a community of artists. He painted it with a bright blue sky and a sunny, buttery yellow — his color for happiness. Fellow painter Paul Gauguin stayed there, but the friendship went badly. It's loved as a cheerful portrait of a hopeful dream, and as a window into his life.
barge-haulers-on-the-volga

Eleven men, bent over and tied to ropes, drag a heavy boat up a river in the burning sun. Repin saw this hard labor himself, and he painted each man as a real person with his own story. It shocked Russian viewers who had rarely seen working people shown with such respect. It's celebrated as a masterpiece of Russian realism and a call for compassion.
a-sunday-afternoon-on-the-island-of-la-grande-jatte

Parisians relax by a river on a sunny Sunday — but the whole picture is made of tiny dots of pure color! Seurat spent two years on it, studying the science of how our eyes mix colors. Standing back, the dots blend into glowing light. This technique, called pointillism, was brand new. It's famous for being both a quiet picnic and a daring experiment.
portrait-of-adele-bloch-bauer-i

A fashionable Viennese lady sits in a glimmering swirl of gold, patterns and eyes, with only her face and hands painted realistically. Klimt covered the canvas in gold leaf, like a Byzantine mosaic. During World War II the painting was taken from its owners, and decades later her family won it back in a famous legal case. Its story is as dramatic as its sparkle.
the-swing

A young woman in a frothy pink dress swings high in a leafy garden while a man hides in the bushes and another gives her a push. Fragonard painted it for a rich French nobleman, and the whole thing is playful, fluffy and fun. Her shoe is flying off into the air! It's the best-known painting of the Rococo style, which celebrated lightness and delight.
grande-odalisque

A woman reclines on a couch with her back to us, looking over her shoulder. Ingres stretched her body longer than is natural, adding extra vertebrae on purpose to create a graceful curve. Critics at the time found it strange, but today it's admired for its elegant lines and silky textures. It's an important example of how artists sometimes break reality for beauty.
a-burial-at-ornans

Courbet painted a funeral in his small hometown on a canvas as big as a history painting. The mourners are ordinary villagers, shown just as they were, without glamor. In 1850 this was shocking, since big canvases were reserved for kings and heroes. It is famous as a landmark of Realism, the idea that everyday people deserve to be painted as important.
ophelia

A young woman floats in a river among flowers, singing as she drifts, based on a scene from Shakespeare's Hamlet. Millais painted every leaf and petal with incredible detail, spending months outdoors beside a river. The model, Elizabeth Siddal, lay in a bathtub filled with water for hours. It's one of the most beloved works of the Pre-Raphaelites, who loved nature and storytelling.
where-do-we-come-from-what-are-we-where-are-we-going

Gauguin painted this huge canvas in Tahiti as a kind of life story, from a baby on the right to an old woman on the left. The title asks three of life's biggest questions. He considered it his masterpiece and said he painted it before planning to end his life, though he lived on. It's famous for its dreamy colors and for asking questions everyone wonders about.
the-birth-of-venus

The Roman goddess Venus rises from the sea on a shell, surrounded by cherubs and carried to shore on the wind. Bouguereau painted her with a smooth, porcelain finish popular in the French Salon. It was a huge hit when new and made him one of the most famous painters in the world. It's a showpiece of academic painting.
ivan-the-terrible-and-his-son-ivan-on-november-16-1581

A Russian tsar cradles his own son, whom he has just struck in a fit of rage, and stares in horror at what he's done. Repin painted the terror and regret on his face so well that it shocked viewers; one even slashed the canvas in 1913 and had to be repaired. It's famous for its raw emotion and for how it shows that power can lead to tragedy.
the-yellow-christ

Women in Breton costumes kneel around a bright yellow crucifix in a golden autumn field. Gauguin was inspired by a wooden carving in a village chapel in Brittany, France. He used flat, bold colors and dark outlines instead of realistic shading. It's a landmark of Synthetism, a style that favored feeling and symbol over copying the world.
the-sleepers

Two women rest in each other's arms on a rumpled bed, caught in a quiet moment. Courbet was a Realist, who wanted to paint life honestly, and the painting was considered scandalous when it was made. Today, it's admired for its soft light and gentle skin tones. It remains an important example of how artists began exploring private moments.
whistler-s-mother

Officially titled 'Arrangement in Grey and Black No. 1', this portrait shows Whistler's mother sitting quietly in profile, with a plain wall and a framed print behind her. Whistler cared about shapes and colors, like musical notes, more than about the story. It became a symbol of motherhood and has been parodied for over a century. It's even been called America's most famous painting.
when-will-you-marry

Two women sit on the ground in Tahiti in bright colorful clothes, one gazing out with a serious look. Gauguin moved to the South Pacific hoping to find a simpler world, and his bold colors and flat shapes helped inspire modern art. The title is a question put to a woman by her neighbors. In 2015 it was reported to have sold for around $300 million, among the highest prices ever.
sunset-at-montmajour

A blazing orange sunset glows over a wild hillside of twisted trees near Arles. For many years, the painting sat forgotten in an attic and was believed to be fake — until 2013, when experts confirmed it as a real Van Gogh. It was a big news story! It's special because it reveals a rare, undiscovered landscape by one of history's most loved artists.
morning-in-a-pine-forest

Four bear cubs play on a fallen tree in a misty pine forest at dawn. Shishkin painted the trees and Savitsky added the bears, though the museum collector later erased Savitsky's name from the signature! The golden light filtering through the fog makes you feel the cool morning air. It is one of the best-loved paintings in Russia, famous even from candy wrappers.
charles-iv-of-spain-and-his-family

Goya painted the royal family of Spain standing in a stiff row, dressed in their grandest clothes. But look closer: the faces look ordinary, even a bit unflattering, and Goya himself is peeking from the back left, just as Velázquez did in 'Las Meninas'. He painted the royals with surprising honesty. It's admired for its sparkling fabrics and for its clever, daring truthfulness.
death-of-sardanapalus

An ancient king lounges on a huge bed, calmly watching his palace be destroyed in a whirlwind of red, gold and chaos. Delacroix based it on a poem by Lord Byron. Critics in 1827 thought it was messy and over the top. But its explosion of color and action thrilled other artists, and it became a landmark of the Romantic movement.
the-painter-s-studio

Courbet shows himself painting a landscape in the center of a huge room, surrounded by friends, models, and the poor on the other side. He called it a 'real allegory' of his life as an artist. The huge scale, usually reserved for history paintings, was a bold statement. It's famous for declaring that a painter's own world is worth painting.
luncheon-of-the-boating-party

Friends laugh, flirt and share wine on a sunny balcony beside the Seine river. Renoir painted his real friends, and the woman at left holding a little dog became his future wife. Light dances over the tablecloth, the fruit, and everyone's straw hats. It's one of the happiest paintings ever made and is why people still smile when they see it.
